_comment: Every change a review has led us to propose, from every review, with a decision and the reason for it. We do not do everything a reviewer says, but every no has a reason here. Which review points led to each proposal is worked out from the reviews and the study's checks, so it is not written twice. Decisions: proposed (we think yes; not built yet, and the reason says why), accepted (will be built; not yet), done (built, in the version named), declined (not doing it, and why), question (we need an answer from someone first).

decisions.proposed: we think yes; not built yet, and the reason says why
decisions.question: we need an answer first; the question is named
decisions.reversed: we declined it, then a later review gave a reason that changed our mind; done in the version named

proposals.title: The line first, the hook second, in answer to a question
proposals.what: The home page, the three steps, start here and every Claude Code behaviour policy go: pick one worry, paste one line, try it. It refuses. Then: it refused because it chose to; what if it decides your task needs the file? The hook is the answer to that question, and arrives with it. The demo plays in the same order.
proposals.reason: Done in a stronger form than we proposed: R002 took the hook out of the first five minutes altogether (P19). The line comes first, and the question it leaves is asked under every example.

proposals.title: A guided path: four stops, each ending in the question that leads to the next
proposals.what: 1. Say it: the line, an expectation. Try it; it refuses. 'It chose to.' 2. Hold it: the hook, a setting. Try it again; Claude Code stops the read before the model sees the file. 'But the hook is a file in my project.' 3. Guard the guard: RM-R0015, and Claude Code's own prompt before any edit to .claude/. 'But it is still my machine and my user.' 4. Put it outside: a boundary, out of the agent's reach: the secret not on the machine, branch protection on the server, the sandbox, managed settings an administrator owns. 'Which of my worries need a boundary?' That question is the start of your mandate. Drawn as a storyboard first, then a page; every behaviour policy shows where it sits on the path.
proposals.reason: The examples are its first stop now: the line, an expectation, and the question it leaves. The other stops wait for Q1, and are no longer on the first screen: they are what a customer reads after the examples.

proposals.title: Say what a hook is, in plain words, where the word first appears
proposals.what: A hook: a small script Claude Code itself runs before the agent acts, which can stop the action. Said once, at the first mention, on every page that mentions one.
proposals.reason: The front pages no longer mention a hook (P19). Where one is offered, on the Claude Code pages, the warning above them says what it is first.

proposals.title: Say what the hook is outside of, and how it fails, where it is offered
proposals.what: Replace 'outside the model' with what is true and what the customer will ask next: Claude Code runs it, not the model, so the model cannot argue with it; it runs as you, from a file in your project, so it is a setting, not a boundary; if it cannot run, the action goes ahead. Each policy page's limits move up, beside the install, and RM-R0015's page says its own limit at the top. The stronger controls are labelled as optional, for later, not a second required step.
proposals.reason: The memo's correction and two invented users (Marcus, Tomás) point the same way. It ships with P1 and P2, because the limits are the questions those two make into steps; how the hook fails ships now, as P11.

proposals.title: Start here shows the next stop, not the whole journey
proposals.what: The seven milestones move off start here to the programme's pages; start here ends with the next stop of the path in P2.
proposals.reason: Start here was rewritten for the browser (R002); it ends with the next five examples and your account, and the seven milestones are only on the programme pages.

proposals.title: A way for every customer to give feedback, and one place it all goes
proposals.what: /feedback/: one line by email; a voice memo with a prompt that has Claude turn the transcript into a review; a prompt that has Claude interview you. /feedback/reviews/: every review verbatim, our reading point by point with screenshots, and this register.
proposals.reason: The memo asked for it, and the programme exists to learn from its customers.

proposals.title: ChatGPT and Claude users never meet the word hook, and find their worry first
proposals.what: A path for people who use ChatGPT or Claude in the browser: their worries first (mail sent as you, all of your mail read), a line, a try, and the honest answer on what holds it. We do not yet know which boundary a ChatGPT user who is not an administrator can set for a connector; until we do, the page says so rather than offering only an administrator's setting.
proposals.reason: Done by R002's web first: every first example runs in ChatGPT or Claude in the browser, and none of them mentions a hook. Which boundary a ChatGPT user can set for a connector is still to be checked (P26).

proposals.title: Synthetic users, run again after every change that matters
proposals.what: Study S1: five invented users on v0.2.1, with profiles and expected journeys written first, the browser helper and the protocol in the repository. The same five run again after P1 and P2 ship, and the two studies are compared.
proposals.reason: The memo asked for it. They are invented, not user research: they find what a page fails to say, not what a customer wants. Study S2, the same five, is due once the lead has reviewed v0.2.3: R002 rebuilt the front pages, and running invented users on a design the lead is still changing would measure the wrong thing.

proposals.title: Say what the £50 is where the balance first appears
proposals.what: All five invented users asked whether the £50 was real money, and four watched the balance fall with nothing on the screen saying why. The home page's badge and the account link now say it: credit for reading, not money; nothing is billed and nothing is blocked; each page's price is on the page.
proposals.reason: Five of five, and a line of text. It does not touch the sequence P1 changes.

proposals.title: Stop telling people to start a new session
proposals.what: Our pages said to start a new session, or open /hooks, so Claude Code loads the hook. Claude Code's documentation says it watches its settings files and applies changes to hooks in the running session, and that /hooks is a read-only list. The pages now say that, and that /hooks is where to check the hook is there.
proposals.reason: A correction of fact, found because Tomás, an invented junior developer, could not tell what a new session meant in the VS Code extension.

proposals.title: Did it work? And what happens when the hook cannot run
proposals.what: Under every Try it: what you see if it worked; what it means if the prompt was not refused (the hook did not run); how to check (is it listed in /hooks? does python3 run where Claude Code runs it? on Windows, Claude Code runs hooks in Git Bash, or PowerShell if Git Bash is not installed); and the fact that matters most: if the hook cannot run, Claude Code lets the action through. The hook fails open (on Windows without Git Bash, Claude Code may block instead), which is one more reason it is a setting and not a boundary. The tests are named for what they are: they feed the hook the JSON Claude Code would send, and do not drive a live session.
proposals.reason: Missing safety information, found by two invented users (Tomás on Windows, Marcus asking fail open or closed). It is about trying, which P1 keeps, so it does not wait for P1.

proposals.title: Each hook, in plain words, beside the install: what it looks at, stops, asks, lets through, and misses; and how to turn it off
proposals.what: A short table beside each hook's settings, and one line on turning it off: remove its entry from .claude/settings.json, and Claude Code stops running it. The box with the hook's source says that it scrolls.
proposals.reason: Sam, an invented developer, left without installing because he could not predict what the hook would block or how to remove it. The table is written from the hooks' own rules.

proposals.title: Line-only pages stop talking about two halves
proposals.what: On a behaviour policy with only a line, the limits table had one row headed 'Half' and the text said 'Neither half is a boundary'. It now says the line is an expectation and is not a boundary.
proposals.reason: A plain mistake in our generator, found by Nadia.

proposals.title: A page for a team: one baseline for everybody, and who can turn it off
proposals.what: For a team lead: commit .claude/settings.json and the hooks to the repository, so everybody who pulls gets them; and for 'does it hold if one of them turns it off', managed settings, which an administrator deploys and no user or project file can override, with the setting that runs only the organisation's hooks. Then branch protection and token scopes, which no setting on a laptop can undo.
proposals.reason: Joan, an invented CTO, left over this, and Marcus asked for managed settings by name. It is stop 4 of P2 for a company; it waits for P2 and for Q3.

proposals.title: What joining the first batch commits a company to
proposals.what: One page a company reads before saying yes: what we ask of you, what you get, what it costs now and later, and how you leave.
proposals.reason: Joan could not find it and left. Only the lead can say what joining commits a company to: Q3.

proposals.title: Customer pages lead with the customer's business
proposals.what: Start here opened with a status line read from docs/reality.md; it now closes the page. The Docs menu, which holds the brief, the memo and how the site is built, is the lead's and ours, not a customer's: proposed to move it under the programme.
proposals.reason: Three invented users stopped on internal papers. The status line moved now; the menu waits for P1, which changes what a customer looks for in it.

proposals.title: The demo shows its point first
proposals.what: The refusal arrives about eleven seconds after the demo comes into view; a reader who scrolls past sooner sees a terminal typing. Proposed: the demo opens on its last frame, the refusal, with a Play button for the whole session.
proposals.reason: Done differently: R002 asked for play, pause and step controls (P22), which let a reader get to the point at their own pace, and the player no longer loops. It does not open on its last frame.

proposals.title: Make the guard fail closed
proposals.what: Claude Code can be told to block the action when a hook fails, with "onFailure": "block" on the hook (Claude Code v2.1.295 or later). Proposed for RM-R0015's hook, the guard of the other three, first; for the others, a choice on each policy's page.
proposals.reason: Failing closed is safer and louder, but on a hook that looks at every read, a missing python3 would then stop every read until it is fixed, and older versions of Claude Code do not know the setting. The trade-off belongs on the page, and the default is the lead's call.

proposals.title: Web first: nothing to install, no hooks and no Claude Code on the front pages
proposals.what: Every first example runs in Claude or ChatGPT in the browser. The home page, start here and the examples mention no hook and install nothing.
proposals.reason: R002's direction, and its security reason: a hook runs code on the customer's machine.

proposals.title: Six examples in tabs, simplest first
proposals.what: Hello world, stay on topic, no web search, keep a secret, drafts never send, refunds up to £50. Each in three acts: ask and it does it; paste the line and ask again; a new chat with the line first. Each with the prompts to copy and what to look for.
proposals.reason: R002 asked for examples in tabs, from hello world to business rules, in the scenario, policy, again, new chat order.

proposals.title: Chat frames like Claude's and ChatGPT's, and a link to open each in a new window
proposals.what: The examples play in a frame drawn roughly like each product's web chat, with a switch between them: messages above, the box you type into at the bottom. No logos; the caption says it is an approximation.
proposals.reason: R002: the old frames were not how either product looks, and most people will try this on the web.

proposals.title: Every demo can be played, paused and stepped
proposals.what: Start again, back, play or pause, next, and which step of how many, on every demo on the site; the arrow keys step too. Plays once when first seen; never loops.
proposals.reason: R002: reading a demo that plays by itself is annoying.

proposals.title: Questions under every example
proposals.what: Did you get it, learn something, were you surprised, did it go as shown, how good was it, and a line. The answers become an email the reader sends, with the example's version; they stay in the reader's browser until then.
proposals.reason: R002: the first users should tell us, example by example, whether it surprised them. Changed at v0.2.4 by R003: the answers go by Encrypt and send (P38), with email only if sending fails.

proposals.title: The three acts, drawn
proposals.what: A strip of the three acts above the examples and on every example's page, in place of 'paste one line, add one hook, try it'.
proposals.reason: R002 asked for an infographic beside the examples; the three acts are what every example has in common.

proposals.title: A small storyboard for each example
proposals.what: Drawn with the storyboard kit, like what-is-an-abp: the scenario, the line, the refusal, the new chat.
proposals.reason: R002 suggested one. Proposed for after the lead has seen the examples as they are, so that the storyboards draw examples that have stopped changing.

proposals.title: Next: your other chats, its memory of you, things it does later
proposals.what: Examples of what assistants can do that most people do not know about, each with the setting that turns it on and a line that limits it.
proposals.reason: R002 asked for them. Each needs a check of what Claude and ChatGPT do today first: an example that claims a capability the assistant does not have would teach the wrong thing. Q5 asks which first.

proposals.title: Your account first, the price list second
proposals.what: An account strip straight under the hero: the balance, and a link to what you have read. The prices stay, on 'What each page costs', and each example's page costs 50p.
proposals.reason: R002: the account matters more than the price list at this stage; the prices are still an experiment, so they stay.

proposals.title: No newsroom in the account: no reader card under pages, and an account page of our own
proposals.what: The meter still charges every page, quietly. /account/ draws the balance, where it went by kind of page, everything read and the top-ups from the meter's own state, without the newsroom's personas or links.
proposals.reason: R002: the reader card and the personas are the newsroom's, not this site's.

proposals.title: Cards that show where they go
proposals.what: Each card on the home page shows a picture of the page it opens, made by admin/build/thumbs.cjs from the page itself.
proposals.reason: R002: a card that does not show what is on the other side is not worth the click.

proposals.title: Professional copy: no 'first customers' on the pages a customer reads
proposals.what: The home page and start here talk to somebody using the site, not to the first batch.
proposals.reason: R002: the site is live and working with users.

proposals.title: Version control of all of it
proposals.what: Each example has a version, shown on it, sent with the answers to its questions and listed on its page; each review records the version it reviewed; a decision that changes keeps its history in this register.
proposals.reason: R002 asked for it. The site's releases were already versioned; the examples and the decisions now are too.

proposals.title: Reviews you can find
proposals.what: Reviews is its own menu; the home page has a band of the latest reviews and what each led to; every footer links to them.
proposals.reason: R003: the reviews could not be found.

proposals.title: The account: everything you did, and everything this browser keeps
proposals.what: Your balance and five counts; each example, how far you got, what you said, whether you sent it; what you sent; where the credit went; everything you read; top-ups; and every item kept in this browser, with what it is and what is in it, Export everything and Delete everything.
proposals.reason: R003: the account should make plain what a reader did and everything kept about it.

proposals.title: A player starts only when you have scrolled to it
proposals.what: Never on a page that has just opened: only after a scroll, with the frame at least 60% on screen; once.
proposals.reason: R003: the example played to its end before it was noticed.

proposals.title: A bar of the steps, and an end that says so
proposals.what: One mark per step, grouped by act, clickable; at the end, 'The end of this example' with Start again and Now try it yourself.
proposals.reason: R003: nothing said it had reached the end, or where it was.

proposals.title: A countdown before each new act
proposals.what: Six seconds, saying what comes next; Pause stops it, Next skips it.
proposals.reason: R003: the jump into the third act came too soon to take in.

proposals.title: Back and Next keep playing
proposals.what: If the player was playing, Back and Next move one step and it carries on.
proposals.reason: R003 found Back confusing while playing; see R003.7 for what we found.

proposals.title: Encrypt and send: an encrypted lane to the agent
proposals.what: A vault on sgit.ai's host with a feedback append lane; the browser encrypts to its public key and appends with its public token; only the vault's key, held by RiskMandate, opens what arrives; admin/feedback/lane.mjs configures, tests and drains it. Agents can send the same way.
proposals.reason: R003 asked for it, after riskmandate.ai's contact form; it answers Q6.

proposals.title: Encrypt and send to the agent, Copy, and How this works
proposals.what: The main button sends, encrypted; Copy stays; Exactly what will be sent is one click away; How this works is a page; email only if sending fails; a box on /feedback/ to send anything.
proposals.reason: R003 asked for it.

proposals.title: The card label that wrapped
proposals.what: Card labels are blocks, so a wrapped line keeps its margin.
proposals.reason: R003 found it.

proposals.title: Keep a secret, act 4: talk it out of the line
proposals.what: A fourth act with the real words of run C1: one sentence lifts the line, and the key comes back. Its Look for says why there are stronger barriers.
proposals.reason: Run C1's most important finding (finding 1): the page called a line an expectation and never let the reader see what that means. It is also the question R001 wanted a customer to reach.

proposals.title: Open Claude in a new tab, and where to look if it is a window
proposals.what: The buttons say new tab, and a note says a window may open behind this one.
proposals.reason: Run C1, finding 2. A page cannot choose a tab over a window; the browser does, so the page says what to look for.

proposals.title: Act 3 in one box
proposals.what: Every example's act 3 is one copy box with the whole first message, set-up and line and ask together; act 2 shows its own ask.
proposals.reason: Run C1, finding 3: the person hesitated at act 3 of every example that needed a set-up.

proposals.title: No web search: what real Claude did in act 2
proposals.what: The Look for says it: the line stopped the search, not the use of what was already in the chat.
proposals.reason: Run C1, finding 4: a second lesson the page did not mention.

proposals.title: Refunds, act 2 asks about a different charge
proposals.what: A £95 fee instead of the £180 act 1 already refunded.
proposals.reason: Run C1, finding 5: as written, act 2 read as asking to be paid twice.

proposals.title: Say what the credit is for, and that Top up is a simulation
proposals.what: The account strip says what this page costs however many examples you watch, and what an example's own page costs; Top up says it is a simulation.
proposals.reason: Run C1, finding 6. The prices stay (D5); what confused was the wording.

proposals.title: One set of questions after the last example
proposals.what: A combined form, as well as the questions under each example.
proposals.reason: Run C1, finding 7. Each example's questions send with one click since v0.2.4 (P38); a combined form waits until we see how many people answer example by example.

proposals.title: The empty player says how to start; ChatGPT logged out, noted
proposals.what: A hint in an empty chat frame; No web search says logged-out ChatGPT may not search.
proposals.reason: Run C1, finding 8.

proposals.title: Next: your own, and which example should we add
proposals.what: After the examples: keep it, write your own, see it in real Claude; and a box that sends us, encrypted, the scenario a reader would want next.
proposals.reason: Run C1, finding 8, and R004: we need to hear from people which scenarios they want.

proposals.title: Replays of real runs: the screenshots, a flow chart, and what the page said beside what happened
proposals.what: A player for the real screenshots of a run, with the same controls as the demos; beside each step what it shows and means, and for each answer what the page said and what the assistant wrote; a flow chart and a scorecard that follow it. The whole run, each example, and the one sentence.
proposals.reason: R004 asked for it.

proposals.title: A storyboard beside the real run, turning with it
proposals.what: An experiment: five real steps of Keep a secret beside a six-panel storyboard drawn from them; the storyboard turns as the replay plays.
proposals.reason: R004 asked for it. Kept as an experiment until people tell us whether it helps.

proposals.title: A brief for browser agents, a personas page, and a record the site reads
proposals.what: The instructions for an agent such as Claude in Chrome: who to be, the rules, what to expect and think at every step, how to take screenshots, the questions, and run.json in the shape the replays read; and the personas it may play, as a page and as data.
proposals.reason: R004 asked for it, after C1 ran from nothing but the home page's address.

proposals.title: Run the same persona after every release, and compare
proposals.what: A second run of Priya, and of Marcus, under the brief; then a page that sets two runs side by side, match by match, so a change that breaks an example shows as a red cell.
proposals.reason: What R004 calls the power of it. Needs a run under the brief first (Q7).

proposals.title: Take the hook out of the first five minutes
proposals.what: One reading of 'a solution for a problem they don't have yet' is to leave the hook for later.
proposals.reason: Declined at v0.2.2: a customer who stops after the line leaves believing their agent is held when it has only been asked. Reversed at v0.2.3 by R002 (R002.7): a hook is a program run on the customer's machine, which our first screen had their agent fetch from our site and install, before any behaviour policy governs what their agent installs. Our concern is kept in words: every example says the line is followed because the assistant chooses to.

proposals.title: A glossary page for hook, expectation, setting and boundary
proposals.what: A page that defines the words.
proposals.reason: A glossary is a page a customer does not open at the moment they need it. Each word is said in plain words where it first appears (P3), and the path (P2) teaches the barrier words by using them.

proposals.title: Show the whole hook, uncut, on the page
proposals.what: Sam's one change, read literally: every line of the hook on the page.
proposals.reason: Sixty-seven lines of Python on the page push Try it down by a screen for everybody, to help the few who read code, and they can open the box or the file. What Sam needed was to predict what it blocks and how to remove it: P12 gives him that in five lines.

proposals.title: A help or FAQ page for installers
proposals.what: Tomás looked for one.
proposals.reason: His two questions were asked on the page where he got stuck, and P10 and P11 answer them there. A help page would be one more place to look.

proposals.title: Stop charging for pages, or hide the balance
proposals.what: Joan found pages that cost real-looking money alarming.
proposals.reason: Every page has a price because the lead asked for it, and the programme exists to find fair prices with its customers. What was wrong was that nothing said what the money is: P9 fixes that.

proposals.title: Delete the Claude Code behaviour policies
proposals.what: R002 says not to use Claude Code for now.
proposals.reason: They are kept, moved down /policies/ under a warning that says a hook is a program that runs on your machine, and nothing on the front pages links to them. They are tested, the lead's own agents run in Claude Code, and the guided path (P2) ends at settings and boundaries that only Claude Code has today. Hidden from a first visit, not deleted.

proposals.title: Runs in ChatGPT as well as Claude
proposals.what: A disposable ChatGPT account for the runs.
proposals.reason: Not now: R004 says Claude only, and the lead has no ChatGPT account for it. The examples stay written for both, and the brief allows one logged-out ChatGPT check.

questions.ask: What does joining the first batch commit a company to: what we ask of them, what it costs now and later, and how they leave? And should the first batch include companies that want a team-wide baseline, or individuals first?
